```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 90)
has_igraph <- requireNamespace("igraph", quietly = TRUE)
```

Collaboration networks are among the oldest objects of network science.
Linking two people when they have worked on the same project, whether a
scientific paper or a film, turns a record of projects into a social
structure in which one can ask who works with whom, who bridges otherwise
separate groups, and how tightly knit a field is. Film casts were one of the
first large collaboration networks studied in this way (Watts & Strogatz,
1998), because every film credits its cast and every credit is public.

A collaboration network is a co-occurrence network with people as items and
projects as transactions. Its construction raises the questions that any
co-occurrence network raises. A film with a large cast links every pair of
its members, so a single production can create hundreds of links that say
little about repeated collaboration; fractional counting gives such a film
the same total weight as a film with two actors (Perianes-Rodriguez et al.,
2016). And a single shared film is weak evidence of a working relationship,
while a pair who share several films have chosen, or been chosen, to work
together again. This case study builds the collaboration network of the
actors in a sample of IMDb films and asks how connected it is, which actors
hold it together, which pairs work together repeatedly, how the choice of
counting changes the picture, and how actors' genres are related.

```{r package}
library(cooccure)
```

## Data

`actors` is a long table with one row per actor and film, drawn from the
IMDb non-commercial datasets for the films in `movies`. It is limited to the
624 actors who appear in at least two of those films. The roles of its
columns are:

- **Item:** `actor`, the actor's name.
- **Transaction:** `tconst`, the film identifier, with `primaryTitle` its
  title.
- **Grouping variable:** `decade`, the film's release decade.
- **Not used here:** `startYear`, `genres` and `averageRating`, which
  describe the film.

A second table, `actor_genres`, lists each of the 624 actors with every genre
of every film they appeared in, one row per actor and genre.

```{r data}
head(actors)
```

Because only actors with at least two films are kept, the casts in this
table are fragments of the full casts.

```{r casts}
with(actors, table(cast_size = table(tconst)))
```

Of the 401 films, 177 keep a single actor from the sample and contribute no
link; a few keep many, up to 38 actors in one film.

## How connected is the collaboration network?

Actors are the items and films the transactions, so `field` names the actor
column and `by` the film column.

```{r network}
collaboration <- cooccurrence(actors, field = "actor", by = "tconst")
summary(collaboration)
```

The 624 actors share 4,353 links, a density of 0.0224: each actor is linked
to 13.9519 others on average, out of 623 possible.
Every weight lies between 1 and 3 films, with a mean of 1.078, so most pairs
have shared a single film. Thirty-four actors have no link: each of their
films kept no other actor from the sample.

Whether the links join the actors into one connected network is a question
for **igraph**.

```{r components, eval = has_igraph}
collaboration_graph <- as_igraph(collaboration)
igraph::count_components(collaboration_graph)
igraph::vcount(igraph::largest_component(collaboration_graph))
```

The network falls into 57 components, of which 34 are the isolated actors. A
single large component holds 495 of the 624 actors; the remaining components
are small groups linked only to each other.

## Which actors hold the network together?

The node table ranks actors by degree, the number of actors they share a
film with.

```{r central}
head(as.data.frame(collaboration, what = "nodes"), 8)
```

The highest degrees belong to actors with only two films each
(`frequency`): Brad Rea, Dawn Michelle King, Kevin LaRosa II, Michael
Runyard and Ricki Lander are each linked to 66 actors. Their two films have
large casts within the sample, and every cast member is linked to every
other. Degree in a collaboration network therefore measures how large an
actor's casts were as much as how widely the actor works.

Betweenness centrality measures something else: how often an actor lies on
the shortest path between two others, and so how far the network depends on
that actor to connect its parts. Edge weights are ignored here, so a path is
counted in films rather than in weights.

```{r betweenness, eval = has_igraph}
head(sort(igraph::betweenness(collaboration_graph, weights = NA),
          decreasing = TRUE), 6)
```

None of the six actors with the highest betweenness is among the actors with
the highest degree. Tony Martin, Hayley Joanne Bacon and the others connect
casts that would otherwise be separate, which large casts alone do not do.

## Which pairs work together repeatedly?

A weight of 2 or more means that two actors share at least two films.
`threshold` keeps those pairs.

```{r repeated}
repeated <- cooccurrence(actors, field = "actor", by = "tconst",
                         threshold = 2)
print(repeated, n = 6)
```

Of the 4,353 links, 338 are repeated collaborations, and only one pair,
Julia Bache-Wiig and Robin Ottersen, shares three films. With the filter, 388
actors have no repeated partner.

The Jaccard index asks a stricter question: of all the films either actor
appears in, what share do they appear in together? Actors with at least three
films in the sample are kept, so that a score rests on more than two films.

```{r jaccard}
regulars <- cooccurrence(actors, field = "actor", by = "tconst",
                         similarity = "jaccard", min_occur = 3)
regulars
```

Only 19 actors have three films in the sample, and they form 7 links.
Julia Bache-Wiig and Robin Ottersen score 1: each appears in the sample only
in the three films they share. Seven of the 19 actors have no link to another
actor with three films.

## Does fractional counting change the network?

Under full counting, a film adds 1 to every pair in its cast. Under
fractional counting, each pair in a film of *n* actors adds 1/(*n* - 1), so
every actor receives a total weight of 1 from each film whatever the size of
the cast.

```{r fractional}
fractional <- cooccurrence(actors, field = "actor", by = "tconst",
                           counting = "fractional")
print(fractional, n = 5)
```

The edges are the same 4,353, but their weights now reflect the size of the
casts. The heaviest pairs, with a weight of 2, are pairs who form the whole
sampled cast of two films each. The actors with the highest degree have a
strength of 2, the same as any actor whose two films each include another
sampled actor, so fractional counting
removes the advantage that large casts gave them under full counting.

For the network of actors with three films, fractional counting changes
nothing.

```{r fractional-regulars}
regulars_fractional <- cooccurrence(actors, field = "actor", by = "tconst",
                                    similarity = "jaccard", min_occur = 3,
                                    counting = "fractional")
all.equal(as_matrix(regulars), as_matrix(regulars_fractional))
```

The two matrices are equal because, once `min_occur = 3` has removed the
other actors, no film keeps more than two of the 19, and for a film of two
actors 1/(*n* - 1) = 1. Fractional counting changes a network only when the
transactions differ in how many items they keep.

## Has collaboration changed across decades?

`split_by` builds one network per decade. Repeated collaborations within a
decade are kept with `threshold = 2`.

```{r decades}
decade_pairs <- cooccurrence(actors, field = "actor", by = "tconst",
                             split_by = "decade", threshold = 2)
as.data.frame(decade_pairs, what = "groups")
```

The number of sampled actors grows from 43 in the 1970s to 353 in the 2010s,
as the sample itself grows from decade to decade. Repeated pairs are most common
relative to the number of actors in the 1970s and 1980s (17 among 43 actors,
47 among 87) and rare in the 1990s and 2020s (6 each). Together the decades
hold 251 repeated pairs (17 + 47 + 6 + 90 + 85 + 6), fewer than the 338 of
the pooled network: 87 pairs repeated their collaboration in a different
decade, and splitting by decade hides them.

## Which genres share actors?

`actor_genres` links actors to genres. Read with genres as items and actors
as transactions, it gives a genre network in which two genres are linked by
the actors who have worked in both.

```{r genres}
career_genres <- cooccurrence(actor_genres, field = "genre", by = "actor",
                              similarity = "jaccard")
print(career_genres, n = 6)
```

The strongest link is between Action and Adventure (0.518, 221 actors),
followed by Action and Drama and by Adventure and Sci-Fi. In the film-level
genre network of the [genre case study](case-imdb-genres.html) the strongest
pair is Adventure and Animation; at the level of careers, the action
adventure dominates. The two networks answer different questions, which
genres are combined in one film and which genres one actor moves between.

## Summary

The actor network is sparse and fragmented into 57 components, with one
large component holding 495 of the 624 actors. High degree in it reflects
large casts, which fractional counting neutralizes, while betweenness picks
out a different set of actors who connect separate casts. Most links rest on
a single film; 338 pairs share two or more, and splitting by decade hides
the 87 pairs whose films fall in different decades. For the counting
methods, see the [guide to counting](counting.html); for per-group networks,
the [guide to comparing groups](comparing-groups.html); and for igraph and
other formats, the [guide to exporting](exporting.html).

## References

Perianes-Rodriguez, A., Waltman, L., & van Eck, N. J. (2016). Constructing
bibliometric networks: A comparison between full and fractional counting.
*Journal of Informetrics*, 10(4), 1178–1195.
<https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joi.2016.10.006>

Watts, D. J., & Strogatz, S. H. (1998). Collective dynamics of 'small-world'
networks. *Nature*, 393(6684), 440–442. <https://doi.org/10.1038/30918>
